general_additionality.general_additionality_approaches_used: Investment analysis (simple cost analysis supported by an investment comparison analysis), barrier analysis, common practice test, and regulatory surplus assessment, applied in accordance with CDM Methodological Tool 01 (Tool for the demonstration and assessment of additionality) as required by VM0033 v2.1 under the VCS v4.5 programme rules. A performance assessment against the project's own baseline trajectory was carried out as corroborating evidence.
general_additionality.general_standardized_additionality_resul: No standardised additionality approach (positive list, performance benchmark, or activity-specific tool) applies to tidal wetland restoration under VM0033 v2.1, so no standardised approach result is reported. Additionality is determined project-specifically through the investment, barrier, and common practice tests, each of which the project passes. The combined conclusion of the three tests is that the project is additional.
general_additionality.general_prior_consideration_details: Carbon credit revenue was considered from the outset and before the project start date of 2023-01-01. The feasibility study was commissioned in April 2021 and completed in June 2021, and modelled carbon credit revenue as the primary funding source for restoration and for the 30-year operating programme. The board of Blue Carbon Kenya Ltd resolved on 2021-11-12 to proceed to project design conditional on a viable carbon finance pathway. A letter of intent was received from Coastal Resilience Buyers Ltd on 2022-08-19, the ex-ante mitigation estimation was completed on 2022-11-01, and the project was listed on the Verra pipeline on 2022-11-15. Prior consideration was notified to Verra within the period required by the VCS programme rules.
general_additionality.general_prior_consideration_evidence: Feasibility study dated 2021-06 (https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_feasibility_study.pdf); minutes and resolution of the Blue Carbon Kenya Ltd board meeting of 2021-11-12 (https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_board_resolution_2021_11_12.pdf); letter of intent from Coastal Resilience Buyers Ltd dated 2022-08-19 (https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_letter_of_intent.pdf); and the dated registry pipeline listing at https://registry.verra.org/app/projectDetail/VCS/4721.
general_additionality.general_other_additionality_evidence: Two further lines of evidence sit outside the standard tests. First, the benefit-sharing agreement signed with three local cooperatives covering 640 community members commits 20% of net carbon revenue to community proceeds; this obligation has no alternative funding source and would not exist in the absence of carbon finance. Second, the non-delivery and political risk insurance policy obtained in support of the forward purchase agreement was underwritten on the basis of expected carbon credit revenue, and the concessional lender's credit paper conditions disbursement on an executed offtake agreement.

financial_additionality.financial_additionality_project_cost_bre: Capital expenditure of USD 4,800,000, comprising nursery establishment (USD 620,000), site preparation and tidal channel rehabilitation (USD 1,450,000), initial planting across approximately 1,200 hectares (USD 1,930,000), monitoring equipment and establishment of 42 permanent sample plots (USD 480,000), and baseline studies, validation, and registry listing costs (USD 320,000). Operating expenditure of USD 720,000 per year, comprising community patrol and ranger salaries (USD 290,000), replanting and maintenance (USD 165,000), monitoring, reporting, and verification fees (USD 145,000), benefit-sharing administration (USD 70,000), and insurance and overheads (USD 50,000), held over the 30-year crediting period. All cost, revenue, price, and return figures in this record are hypothetical.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_project_revenue_: Revenue other than carbon credit revenue totals approximately USD 95,000 per year: a community ecotourism concession fee (USD 55,000), a co-managed fisheries landing levy shared with the three partner cooperatives (USD 28,000), and research access and training fees (USD 12,000). No public subsidy or grant income is recognised as revenue; grant and concessional debt are treated as funding sources rather than project revenue. Expected carbon credit revenue of approximately USD 1,132,320 per year (53,920 tCO2e at the expected price of USD 21.00 per tCO2e) is excluded from this breakdown and assessed separately.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_financial_indica: Net present value (NPV) at a 10% real discount rate, applied consistently across the simple cost analysis, the investment comparison analysis, and the sensitivity analysis. Internal rate of return was not used as the primary indicator because the project generates no positive net annual cash flow in the absence of carbon credit revenue, so no project IRR exists for the without-carbon case.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_financial_benchm: Benchmark analysis was assessed for applicability and not applied. A benchmark comparison requires a calculable project IRR excluding carbon credit revenue. Excluding carbon credit revenue the project returns USD 95,000 of revenue against USD 720,000 of operating costs in every year of the 30-year crediting period, following USD 4,800,000 of upfront capital expenditure, so annual net cash flow is negative throughout and no IRR can be calculated. The benchmark that would have been applied, had the approach been available, is a country- and sector-specific expected return on equity of 11.5% for long-dated coastal land-use investments in Kenya. Simple cost analysis was used instead, as provided for in CDM Methodological Tool 01 where a project has no significant revenue other than carbon credit revenue.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_investment_analy: Simple cost analysis, supported by an investment comparison analysis against the most plausible alternative use of the project area. Benchmark analysis was not applied, for the reason recorded in the benchmark calculations field.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_investment_compa: The project was compared against the most plausible alternative use of the project area: conversion of approximately 180 hectares of the landward zone to semi-intensive shrimp aquaculture, with continued informal fuelwood and building-pole harvesting across the remainder of the creek. The alternative was modelled over the same 30-year period at the same 10% real discount rate, assuming capital expenditure of USD 2,100,000 for pond construction and stocking, operating costs of USD 1,350,000 per year, and gross revenue of USD 2,050,000 per year at prevailing regional farm-gate prices, giving net annual cash flow of USD 700,000 and an NPV of approximately positive USD 4.50 million. The project, excluding carbon credit revenue, returns negative net annual cash flow of USD 625,000 and an NPV of approximately negative USD 10.69 million on the same basis.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_financial_benchm: No benchmark comparison result is reported, because the benchmark approach was not applied. The equivalent conclusion is drawn from the simple cost analysis: the project's NPV excluding carbon credit revenue is negative USD 10.69 million, which falls below any non-negative financial benchmark that could reasonably be applied to a 30-year coastal restoration investment in Kenya, including the 11.5% return-on-equity benchmark considered. The project is not financially viable without carbon credit revenue.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_investment_compa: The project is substantially less economically attractive than the alternative scenario: negative USD 10.69 million NPV excluding carbon credit revenue, against positive USD 4.50 million for conversion to semi-intensive aquaculture, a difference of approximately USD 15.19 million in present value terms. A profit-seeking land manager would not choose the project over the alternative in the absence of carbon finance. Including carbon credit revenue the project's NPV rises to approximately negative USD 0.02 million, which still does not exceed the alternative; the residual gap is met by grant and concessional debt finance rather than by commercial return.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_sensitivity_anal: The conclusion is robust to reasonable variation in every critical assumption. Operating costs were varied by plus or minus 20% (USD 576,000 to USD 864,000 per year), the real discount rate between 8% and 12%, non-carbon revenue by plus or minus 50% (USD 47,500 to USD 142,500 per year), and the expected carbon price by plus or minus 30% (USD 14.70 to USD 27.30 per tCO2e). Across every combination tested, the project's NPV excluding carbon credit revenue remains negative, ranging from approximately negative USD 8.3 million to negative USD 14.0 million. Including carbon credit revenue at central cost assumptions and a 10% discount rate, NPV ranges from approximately negative USD 3.2 million at the low carbon price to positive USD 3.2 million at the high carbon price, confirming that the project's financial viability is determined almost entirely by carbon credit revenue.

Operating cost ranges were derived from the three-year operating record of two comparable East African coastal restoration programmes and from local wage and marine fuel indices. The 8% to 12% discount rate band is the range applied to long-dated land-use investments in Kenya by the project's concessional lender. The carbon price range reflects the five-year observed spread of transacted prices for nature-based removals of comparable vintage and geography, and brackets both the expected price of USD 21.00 and the contracted forward price of USD 18.50 per tCO2e. The full model, with annual cash flow tables for each scenario, is at https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_financial_additionality_model.xlsx and is summarised in Section 3.4 of the Project Design Document.
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_simple_cost_anal: Over the 30-year crediting period the project incurs USD 4,800,000 of upfront capital expenditure and USD 21,600,000 of undiscounted operating costs, against USD 2,850,000 of undiscounted non-carbon revenue, giving an undiscounted net cost of USD 23,550,000 and a net present value of negative USD 10.69 million at a 10% real discount rate. The project produces no commercially saleable output other than carbon credits: restored mangrove is placed under a protection and co-management agreement and is not harvested. The present value of expected carbon credit revenue at USD 21.00 per tCO2e is USD 10.67 million, which offsets approximately 99.8% of the funding deficit and leaves the project marginally cash-negative even with carbon finance. The project is therefore economically unattractive without carbon credit income.

Audited cost schedule and contractor quotations for nursery, channel rehabilitation, and planting works; community employment and patrol agreements; the ecotourism concession agreement and three years of fisheries landing levy records; and the verification fee schedule agreed with SCS Global Services. Inputs are consistent with the project finance record for this project (expected initial costs USD 4,800,000, expected annual costs USD 720,000, expected annual revenue USD 1,132,320, total funding required USD 8,400,000). Supporting workbook: https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_financial_additionality_model.xlsx
financial_additionality.financial_additionality_carbon_finance_d: The board resolution of 2021-11-12 made the final investment decision conditional on a viable carbon finance pathway. Two commercial banks declined to finance the project on conventional terms, by letters dated 2022-03-04 and 2022-05-17, citing the absence of a saleable output. The concessional lender's credit paper conditions disbursement on an executed carbon offtake agreement. The forward purchase agreement effective 2026-03-01 commits USD 2,775,000 against 150,000 tCO2e of 2026-2028 vintages at USD 18.50 per tCO2e, with 40% prepaid on satisfaction of conditions precedent; that prepayment funds the restoration programme directly. Secured funding of USD 5,650,000 against a total requirement of USD 8,400,000 is contingent on continued carbon market participation.

barriers.barriers_alternative_scenario_barrier_de: The most plausible alternative to the project, conversion of the landward zone to semi-intensive shrimp aquaculture with continued informal harvesting elsewhere in the creek, faces none of the barriers identified for the project. Pond construction uses established technology available from contractors in Kilifi County, is routinely financed by commercial banks against pond assets and harvest receivables, requires only a county land-use permit and an effluent licence on a published approval timeline, and generates positive cash flow from the second production cycle. The continuation of informal fuelwood and building-pole harvesting requires no capital, no permit, no technical capacity, and no community agreement, and is already occurring. At least one plausible alternative therefore does not face the project's financial, institutional, or technical capacity barriers.
barriers.barriers_barrier_demonstration: Three barriers prevent implementation, and carbon credit revenue is the key factor in overcoming each. (i) Financial barrier: two commercial banks declined to lend on conventional terms, by letters dated 2022-03-04 and 2022-05-17, on the grounds that the project has no saleable output and no collateralisable receivable; carbon credit revenue with a present value of USD 10.67 million is the only identified source capable of covering the USD 10.69 million present value deficit, and the forward purchase receivable is the asset against which concessional debt was ultimately advanced. (ii) Institutional barrier: the activity required a co-management agreement with Kenya Forest Service and benefit-sharing agreements with three community cooperatives, negotiated over 14 months and concluded only once a funded benefit stream, 20% of net carbon revenue, could be committed; without that stream the cooperatives declined to restrict harvesting access. (iii) Information and technical capacity barrier: no local capability existed for tidal wetland carbon accounting, soil organic carbon sampling, or permanent plot monitoring; the USD 145,000 annual MRV programme and the associated training of community monitoring teams are funded entirely from carbon revenue and have no alternative funding source.
barriers.barriers_chosen_barrier_explanation_and_: The financial barrier was selected as the primary barrier for the analysis, because the institutional and technical capacity barriers are themselves resolved by expenditure that only carbon revenue funds, and so are not independent of it. Result: carbon credit revenue with a present value of USD 10.67 million converts a project carrying a present value deficit of USD 10.69 million into one that is fundable alongside the USD 5,650,000 of secured grant and concessional finance against the USD 8,400,000 total requirement. No alternative source of finance was identified that would close the gap, and no commercial lender was willing to finance the activity absent a carbon offtake. Carbon credit revenue is therefore the decisive factor in overcoming the barrier.
barriers.barriers_implementation_barriers: Financial barriers; institutional barriers covering land tenure, carbon rights, and co-management approvals; and information and technical capacity barriers covering the absence of local tidal wetland MRV capability. Technological barriers were assessed and found not to apply, because the project deliberately uses proven planting and hydrological restoration practice rather than novel technology.
barriers.barriers_other_additionality_approach_na: Not applicable. The project demonstrates additionality using the investment analysis, barrier analysis, and common practice tests set out in CDM Methodological Tool 01 as applied by VM0033 v2.1, supplemented by the regulatory surplus assessment required under VCS v4.5. No other standardised approach, positive list, or activity-specific tool is relied upon.
barriers.barriers_other_barrier_types: Two barrier types outside the standard categories were assessed. Seasonal access: restoration sites in the upper creek are reachable only by boat at high tide for part of the year, constraining the planting and monitoring calendar. Community security: the project depends on voluntary community patrols in an area with a recorded history of dispute over fishing access, which affects the reliability of protection outcomes. Both were identified through the participatory rural appraisal and household socioeconomic survey conducted in 2022 and were assessed as material to implementation scheduling and cost, but not prohibitive on their own.

common_practice.common_practice_common_practice_document: Comparable activity analysis covering the Kenyan coast (Kilifi, Kwale, Lamu, Mombasa, and Tana River counties), drawing on Kenya Forest Service mangrove restoration records for 2013 to 2022, the status review published under the National Mangrove Ecosystem Management Plan 2017-2027, Verra and Gold Standard registry extracts for tidal wetland projects in East Africa as at 2022-10-31, county forestry and fisheries department records, and Landsat and Sentinel-2 change detection used to identify areas under active restoration. Dataset and analysis: https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_common_practice_analysis.pdf
common_practice.common_practice_common_practice_test_det: The common practice test was applied in accordance with Step 4 of CDM Methodological Tool 01, as required by VM0033 v2.1 under the VCS v4.5 programme rules. The threshold for market penetration is set by the methodology and the applicable carbon-crediting programme, not by the project proponent. The test compares the project activity, hydrological restoration and assisted natural regeneration of degraded tidal mangrove above 1,000 hectares under long-term community co-management, against similar activities of comparable scale in the same geography and regulatory environment.
common_practice.common_practice_first_of_kind_details: The project is not claimed to be first of its kind. Community-based mangrove restoration has precedent on the Kenyan coast, most notably at Gazi Bay, and the project deliberately adopts proven planting and co-management practice rather than novel technology. It differs from those precedents in scale, approximately 1,200 hectares against tens to low hundreds of hectares, and in rehabilitating tidal channel hydrology before planting rather than planting directly into degraded substrate. Neither difference is presented as a first-of-kind innovation.
common_practice.common_practice_first_of_kind_documentat: Not applicable; no first-of-kind claim is made. The comparison against precedent restoration activity on the Kenyan coast, including the Gazi Bay project, is documented in the common practice analysis at https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_common_practice_analysis.pdf
common_practice.common_practice_market_penetration_thres: Below 20% market penetration, as defined by the applicable methodology and carbon-crediting programme rules. The analysis identified approximately 2,100 hectares restored or under active restoration against an estimated 24,000 hectares of degraded mangrove across the five coastal counties, a penetration of approximately 9%. The project activity is below the threshold and is therefore not common practice.

counterfactual_scenario.counterfactual_scenario_counterfactual_s: In the absence of carbon finance the project area would continue to degrade. The baseline projects continued loss of approximately 1.9% of remaining mangrove extent per year from fuelwood and building-pole harvesting, together with conversion of approximately 180 hectares of the landward zone to aquaculture ponds within the first decade, leaving the area a net source of approximately 14,800 tCO2e per year rather than a net sink. Measured against this baseline, the project's expected net mitigation of approximately 53,920 tCO2e per year, comprising avoided baseline emissions and removals into restored biomass and sediment carbon, is additional. The baseline is conservative: it assumes no acceleration of harvesting pressure from coastal population growth, and credits the existing statutory harvesting prohibition with its observed rather than its nominal level of enforcement.

The baseline was constructed under VM0033 v2.1 and is project-specific. Inputs are 2013-2022 Landsat and Sentinel-2 change detection over the project area and a 5 km reference region, 42 permanent sample plots stratified by elevation and salinity, soil organic carbon sampling to 1 m depth, household fuelwood consumption surveys covering the three partner communities, and county records of aquaculture permit applications. The baseline is subject to re-assessment at each 10-year baseline period under VCS v4.5 and on any revision of VM0033. Full analysis: https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_baseline_and_counterfactual_analysis.pdf

Three alternative scenarios were assessed. (1) Continuation of the pre-project situation: unmanaged harvesting and progressive degradation of the creek system, requiring no capital, no permit, and no agreement. (2) Conversion of approximately 180 hectares of the landward zone to semi-intensive shrimp aquaculture, with continued informal harvesting elsewhere, financed commercially and permitted at county level. (3) The project activity implemented without carbon finance and funded from grants alone, rejected as not plausible because identified grant and concessional commitments total USD 5,650,000 against a total requirement of USD 8,400,000, and no grant source was identified that would fund the USD 720,000 annual operating cost across a 30-year protection and monitoring programme. Scenario 1 was selected as the baseline, as the most plausible outcome and the most conservative of the three.
counterfactual_scenario.counterfactual_scenario_alternative_scen: Evidence that the alternatives do not face the project's barriers: three commercial bank term sheets issued for aquaculture developments in Kilifi County between 2020 and 2022; the published county aquaculture licensing schedule and permit issuance records showing routine approval within the stated timeline; and household survey data recording ongoing unlicensed fuelwood harvesting that requires neither finance nor permission. These are contrasted with the two financing declines received by the project, dated 2022-03-04 and 2022-05-17, and with the 14-month co-management negotiation record. Compiled at https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_alternative_scenario_barrier_evidence.pdf

performance_additionality.performance_additionality_performance_ba: The project's expected performance exceeds the applicable baseline benchmark in every year of the crediting period. Against a baseline in which the project area is a net source of approximately 14,800 tCO2e per year, the project scenario yields expected net mitigation of approximately 53,920 tCO2e per year and approximately 1,617,600 tCO2e over the 30-year crediting period. The performance assessment corroborates the investment and barrier analyses and is not relied upon in their place.

Performance was measured under VM0033 v2.1 using 42 permanent sample plots stratified by elevation and salinity, allometric equations for East African mangrove species, soil organic carbon sampling to 1 m depth on a three-year cycle, and annual Sentinel-2 change detection over the project area and the 5 km reference region. Ex-ante estimates were validated by SCS Global Services during initial project validation in May 2023. Assessment: https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_performance_benchmark_assessment.pdf
performance_additionality.performance_additionality_performance_in: Net annual carbon stock change across the project area, expressed in tCO2e per year, covering above-ground and below-ground biomass and soil organic carbon, net of project emissions and leakage, and measured against the VM0033 baseline trajectory for the same area.
performance_additionality.performance_additionality_performance_th: The project must demonstrate net annual carbon stock change above the baseline trajectory for the same area, which is a net loss under continued degradation. The threshold is therefore the project-specific baseline trajectory rather than a sector-wide benchmark value, because VM0033 v2.1 does not define a standardised performance benchmark for tidal wetland restoration.

Valid for the current baseline period. Under VCS v4.5 the baseline must be re-assessed at the end of each 10-year baseline period within the 2023-01-01 to 2052-12-31 crediting period, with the next re-assessment due by 2032-12-31, and the threshold must also be revisited on any revision of VM0033.

regulatory_additionality.regulatory_additionality_regulatory_surp: The applicable legal framework comprises the Forest Conservation and Management Act 2016, the Environmental Management and Co-ordination Act as amended, the Fisheries Management and Development Act 2016, the Climate Change Act 2016 as amended in 2023, and the Kilifi County land-use framework. Mangroves in the project area are gazetted public forest under Kenya Forest Service management and unlicensed cutting is prohibited, but no instrument requires any party to undertake active restoration, tidal channel rehabilitation, or long-term protection of the kind the project implements, and no party bears a legal obligation to deliver the project activity. The National Mangrove Ecosystem Management Plan 2017-2027 sets restoration targets for the coastal counties but is a policy instrument without binding force or allocated funding. Enforcement of the existing harvesting prohibition is documented as limited, with continued unlicensed harvesting recorded throughout the baseline period, so the baseline reflects actual rather than nominal enforcement. The project activity is not legally required and is therefore regulatory surplus.
regulatory_additionality.regulatory_additionality_legal_regulator: Legal opinion on applicable law, carbon rights, and regulatory surplus prepared by Kenyan counsel and dated 2022-09-30 (https://example.org/docs/mida_creek_legal_regulatory_analysis.pdf); the co-management agreement with Kenya Forest Service; the enforcement record review covering county and Kenya Forest Service prosecution and permit data for 2013 to 2022; and the carbon concession contract and carbon rights evidence recorded in the project disclosures.
regulatory_additionality.regulatory_additionality_regulatory_addi: Legal analysis of applicable national and county law by qualified Kenyan counsel, combined with an assessment of actual enforcement levels measured against documented harvesting rates over the 2013 to 2022 baseline period, applied in accordance with the regulatory surplus requirements of VCS v4.5 and Step 1 of CDM Methodological Tool 01. No positive list of activities applies to this project type.

lockin_risk.lockin_risk_applicable_activities_techno: Hydrological restoration and assisted natural regeneration of degraded tidal mangrove ecosystems, including tidal channel rehabilitation, nursery propagation and enrichment planting of native species (Rhizophora mucronata, Avicennia marina, Ceriops tagal, and Sonneratia alba), and community co-management with patrol-based protection. No combustion, process, or energy-conversion technology is deployed.
lockin_risk.lockin_risk_country_ltleds_compatibility: Compatible. Kenya's updated Nationally Determined Contribution and national climate change action planning identify mangrove and coastal ecosystem restoration as a priority mitigation and adaptation measure, and the National Mangrove Ecosystem Management Plan 2017-2027 sets restoration targets for Kilifi County to which the project contributes. The activity restores a natural carbon sink and creates no dependence on emitting infrastructure, so it is consistent with any long-term low-emission development pathway for the host country.
lockin_risk.lockin_risk_project_scale: Approximately 1,200 hectares of degraded mangrove within the Mida Creek system, with expected net mitigation of approximately 53,920 tCO2e per year and approximately 1,617,600 tCO2e across the 30-year crediting period. Project assets are ecological rather than built, and no long-lived emitting infrastructure is constructed.
lockin_risk.lockin_risk_technology_emissions_intensi: Net negative. The restored ecosystem is a net carbon sink across the crediting period, against a baseline in which the same area is a net source. Residual project emissions are limited to fuel for boat-based monitoring and patrols and to nursery operations, estimated at under 0.5% of gross annual removals. No higher-emitting technology is deployed, displaced, or locked in. The only reversal pathway is ecological degradation if protection ceased, which the buffer pool contribution and the long-term co-management agreement are designed to address.
